etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English susteinen, sustenen, from Old French sustenir (French soutenir), from Latin sustineō, sustinēre (“to uphold”), from sub- (“from below, up”) + teneō (“hold”, verb).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To maintain, or keep in existence.

quote.citation: 1949 June 8, George Orwell [pseudonym; Eric Arthur Blair], chapter 9, in Nineteen Eighty-Four: A Novel, London: Secker & Warburg, →OCLC; republished [Australia]: Project Gutenberg of Australia, August 2001:
quote.text: All the beliefs, habits, tastes, emotions, mental attitudes that characterize our time are really designed to sustain the mystique of the Party and prevent the true nature of present-day society from being perceived.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Nehemiah 9:21:
quote.text: Yea, forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing; their clothes waxed not old, and their feet swelled not.

quote.citation: 1937, Robert Byron, The Road to Oxiana‎[1], London: Macmillan, Part 2, page 59:
quote.text: We rode five farsakhs today, sustained by a single bowl of curds and tortured by the wooden saddles.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To encourage or sanction (something). (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:)
(transitive) To experience or suffer (an injury, etc.).

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: […]  if you omitThe offer of this time, I cannot promiseBut that you shall sustain moe new disgraces,With these you bear already.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Seventh Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, lines 592-593:
quote.text: Shall Turnus then such endless Toil sustain,In fighting Fields, and conquer Towns in vain:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To confirm, prove, or corroborate; to uphold.

quote.citation: 1876, Henry Martyn Robert, Pocket Manual of Rules of Order for Deliberative Assemblies‎[2], Chicago: Griggs, published 1885, Section 61 (e), page 167:
quote.text: After the vote is taken, the Chairman states that the decision of the Chair is sustained, or reversed, as the case may be.

definitions.definition: (law, of a judge) To allow, accept, or admit (e.g. an objection or motion) as valid.
To keep from falling; to bear; to uphold; to support.
To aid, comfort, or relieve; to vindicate.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii]:
quote.text: When I desir’d their leave that I might pity him, they took from me the use of mine own house, charg’d me on pain of perpetual displeasure neither to speak of him, entreat for him, nor any way sustain him.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Sixth Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, lines 1122-1123:
quote.text: His Sons, who seek the Tyrant to sustain,And long for Arbitrary Lords again,

definitions.definition: (music) A mechanism which can be used to hold a note, as the right pedal on a piano.

quote.citation: 2011, Chuck Eddy, Rock and Roll Always Forgets, page 265:
quote.text: To call this music bland is to ignore the down-the-drain vocal fade-aways, the extended sax sustains  […]
